For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
**Verdict: not ready to go to decision-makers.** The recommendation is clear, but the £193k figure it rests on is overstated, and the document leaves out the biggest risk to it.

## Problems that change the answer

**1. Cannibalisation is missing.** Section 2 says 31% of current standard members (about 2,976 of 9,600) visit only in the off-peak window, and another 22% visit mostly off-peak. Section 6 lets members switch with one month's notice. Each one who moves from £42 to £29 costs £13 a month, or £156 a year.
- The £193,200 net is wiped out if about 1,240 members switch, which is roughly 42% of the exclusive off-peak group.
- Even 20% switching costs about £93k a year.
- The document never mentions this, and Section 7 lists only "perceived unfairness".

**2. The projection assumes all 1,200 members join on day one and stay all year.** £417,600 is 1,200 × £29 × 12. Recruitment will ramp up through the year, and members will churn. Average membership in year one is more likely around 600 or fewer. At 600 members, revenue is about £209k, which is less than the £224k class cost. The year-one net could be negative before cannibalisation is considered.

**3. The retention claim is correlation presented as cause.** Members who attend classes churn less, but engaged members are both more likely to attend classes and more likely to stay. That does not show that adding classes will lower churn. The document also:
- says managers report daytime classes are often under-filled, so the first step is to fill existing classes, not add 24 new ones a week
- includes no retention benefit in the revenue figures, so the £224k is treated as pure cost
- says churn "should" fall to 2.1% with no evidence

The cost is certain, and the benefit is neither measured nor modelled. The author's "investment, not a cost" framing isn't supported.

**4. The 300-per-club figure isn't shown to follow from the survey.** 19% of 640 is about 120 people who said "definitely" or "probably", and stated intent usually overstates actual sign-ups. The document gives no catchment population, no discount for intent versus behaviour, and no breakdown of "definitely" versus "probably". "Consistent with the survey" and "conservative" are assertions, not calculations. The survey also tested only £29, so it says nothing about sensitivity to the budget gyms' £22–25.

## Other issues to fix

- **Access hours contradict each other.** Section 1 says before 4 pm on weekdays. Section 6 says until 5 pm. This also affects the capacity case, because 4–5 pm is close to the peak.
- **Capacity evidence covers only weekday daytimes (about 30%).** The offer includes all day at weekends, and no weekend utilisation is given. Members migrating from standard add to the load too.
- **The "no price war" reasoning doesn't follow.** Budget gyms already undercutting £29 is a reason the target groups may not convert, not a reason competitors won't respond.
- **The risks section is thin.** It should cover cannibalisation, ramp-up, class cost versus uptake, and what happens if sign-ups fall short.
- **The launch date has passed.** The document is dated August 2026 and proposes launch on 1 October 2026, but today is 13 November 2026. Update the date or say whether launch has been rescheduled.

## What I'd do before sending

1. Model cannibalisation with low, medium and high switching scenarios, and show break-even.
2. Rebuild the revenue line monthly with a ramp-up and churn, and show net revenue under pessimistic, central and optimistic cases.
3. Show how the 300-per-club figure derives from catchment size and a conversion discount.
4. Either trial the extra classes or phase them in once existing daytime classes are reasonably full, and drop the causal retention claim or label it a hypothesis.
5. Consider ways to limit downgrades, such as a notice period, a minimum term, or restricting off-peak to new joiners for a period.
6. Fix the hours inconsistency, add weekend utilisation, and update the dates.

The idea may well be sound, but the document currently overstates the case. Once the numbers include cannibalisation and a realistic ramp, the recommendation could change, for example to a phased pilot at one or two clubs.
